displayQuote: Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced

meta.title: Who really said "Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — James Baldwin wrote it, in his 1962 essay “As Much Truth As One Can Bear” for The New York Times Book Review. His original used a semicolon.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely James Baldwin: his 1962 New York Times Book Review essay “As Much Truth As One Can Bear.” The original used a semicolon, not a comma.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Baldwin wrote this in his essay “As Much Truth As One Can Bear,” published in The New York Times Book Review on 14 January 1962. The wording is genuine — though his original used a semicolon (“can be changed; but nothing”), where the popular version substitutes a comma.

trail: Quote Investigator traces the line to Baldwin’s essay “As Much Truth As One Can Bear” and confirms the 1962 New York Times Book Review printing via ProQuest.
Wikiquote’s sourced section cites the same essay and date, and notes its reprint in The Cross of Redemption (2010/2011).
Snopes rates the attribution genuine, quoting the essay’s concluding paragraph on the writer’s duty to confront the world.
source.excerptNote: Baldwin’s original punctuation uses a semicolon between the clauses; the widely shared version replaces it with a comma.

source.rightsNote: The essay was first published in 1962 and remains under U.S. copyright; the line also appears in the 2010 collection The Cross of Redemption. Rights rest with the Estate of James Baldwin and its publishers — this is a genuine, but not public-domain, quotation.

author.name: James Baldwin
author.heading: About James Baldwin
author.bio: James Baldwin was one of the twentieth century’s most searching essayists, the author of Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953), Notes of a Native Son (1955), Giovanni’s Room (1956) and The Fire Next Time (1963). Writing on race, sexuality and American identity, he made the act of facing uncomfortable truth the moral center of his work — which is exactly what this line, from a 1962 essay on the writer’s responsibility, distills.

misattribution.heading: The record
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is correct — this is really Baldwin. What travels incorrectly is the punctuation and, occasionally, the exact source.

items.why: Baldwin’s original reads “can be changed; but nothing can be changed until it is faced” — a semicolon, per Quote Investigator and Wikiquote. The version circulated on social media almost always swaps in a comma.

The line is regularly shared with no citation, or loosely as “Baldwin said.” The documented source is the essay “As Much Truth As One Can Bear,” The New York Times Book Review, 14 January 1962, as Snopes confirms.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Baldwin — written in 1962; the only correction is the semicolon he actually used, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Baldwin wrote the line in a short essay on the writer’s vocation — the obligation, as he put it, to speak out about the world as it is rather than as one would wish it. The sentence has since outgrown its origin, becoming a touchstone for movements from recovery to racial justice precisely because it refuses easy optimism: facing a thing guarantees nothing, but it is the non-negotiable first step.
context.pull: Nothing can be changed until it is faced.
